subject: Let a funder start from a task that already exists
body:
Posting a second task usually means the same shape as the first with one thing
changed, and rebuilding it from defaults invites a typo in the economics rather
than in the scene. Six existing tasks are offered as starting points, each
carrying its payload, landmark, room, rate, slot count and difficulty across.

Nothing is posted until the funder signs — a template fills the form, it does
not create anything.

subject: Light each room the way that room is lit
body:
A kitchen counter under the same cold key as a workshop bench reads as the same
room with different furniture. Each room now carries its own key, fill and
hemisphere: the light it would actually have, what bounces back off its
materials, and the ambient above it. Keyed by the scenario the contract stores,
so the lighting is derivable from chain state like everything else about a scene.

Held narrow on purpose — the scene is a measuring instrument and the datum has
to stay legible under all seven, so none of them is far enough from neutral to
change how a placement reads.

The detector was right to flag thirteen new colours. They are light sources
rather than surfaces, which is a real new category and not an excuse, so they
are declared as their own scene-* group in DESIGN.md with the reason, instead of
being quietly added to the interface palette.

subject: Give log lines a message, or Railway renders them blank
body:
The wrapper was firing correctly — the line count and timestamps matched the
requests exactly, three then four — and every row in the log viewer was empty.
Railway renders a JSON stdout line by its `message` field, and these had
`event` instead, so a working logger looked like a broken one.

The rendered summary now sits beside the structured fields rather than replacing
them, so the line is readable by a person scrolling and still parseable by a
tool.

subject: Log every write, and tell a contributor their own share
body:
When a submission failed in production the only record was whatever the platform
happened to capture: no request id, nothing to tie a client's report to a server
event, nothing a log tool could group by. The four write routes now emit one
JSON line each with an id, the route, the status and the duration — measured
from the handler actually running, and a thrown error is logged and rethrown
rather than swallowed. No bodies are logged: trajectory samples are the product
and an address is personal.

The cap table lists every contributor's share and a contributor had to find
their own address in it. The connected wallet's row is highlighted and a line
above says what a licence would pay them, shown only when they are actually in
the table — telling someone who never contributed that they would receive
nothing is noise.

subject: Show how everyone did a task, not just how well
body:
The histogram says how the scores fell. It cannot say whether the good runs
share a route, whether there are two equally good approaches, or whether the
poor ones wander — and that is the thing someone deciding whether a corpus is
worth licensing actually needs to see about its diversity.

Every accepted approach is drawn on one plate, best brightest, the rest
receding. Hovering a row lifts its path out of the bundle. Paths are
downsampled by even stride rather than truncated, so a long run keeps its whole
shape rather than its first two seconds, and the final point is always kept
because that point is the placement.

subject: Let the slot tally read as having moved
body:
The blocks light in sequence rather than all at once, so a tally that just took
a slot shows it taking one. The per-block delay is capped and scaled so a full
bar finishes in 360ms rather than crawling — 24 blocks at 15ms apart, one block
at 18ms.

subject: Stop losing a measured run to a reload
body:
Between the measurement and the transaction there is a wallet prompt, and that
is where runs were being lost: a reload, an extension taking focus, a tab the
browser restored, and the samples were gone with no way back. By then the work
is real — the arm has been driven and the score is decided — so losing it loses
the operator's actual labour.

A measured run is kept in sessionStorage, offered back once on return to the
same task, and cleared the moment the chain confirms it or the operator
discards it. Deliberately session-scoped and deliberately never a substitute
for the chain: a draft is only ever an unsent run, and one older than an hour is
not offered at all.

subject: Say what a task is actually about, on the hub
body:
A row said 'Put the toothpaste into the upper drawer' and nothing about what
would be on the table. The catalogue already resolves the payload, the landmark
and the room for every task, so each row and card now names them — Toothpaste,
Drawer, Bathroom Vanity — before you commit to opening the station.

Inline rather than on hover, so it works on a phone and for anyone who never
hovers.

subject: Put the payouts on the page that claims them
body:
The landing page asserts that a run is recorded and paid in one transaction, and
then showed none of it. The activity feed already existed on the hub, reading
the contract's own log; the eight most recent payouts now sit above the footer,
where the claim is made.

subject: Age the trail, hold the wrist, mark the workspace
body:
The tool path was one flat colour, which says where the payload has been. It now
fades along its own length so the newest quarter reads brightest — where it just
was is the part worth reading while driving. Per-vertex colour, written only
over the range actually drawn.

A completely still arm reads as a broken one, so the wrist carries a very small
slow drift while nothing is held: about the amount a real servo holding position
moves, not an animation. It stops the moment the jaws take the payload.

The canvas takes a crosshair, because the thing under the pointer is a
workspace being measured, not a page being browsed.

subject: Document the print ramp instead of drifting into it
body:
The detector was right: a 10px caption and a literal #4a4a4a are drift, however
reasonable they look. The caption moved to the documented 12px step and the
colour to a token.

Print is the one place this system inverts — ink on white — so the six inverted
values are now written into DESIGN.md as an intentional addition, with the note
that they are the same tonal relationships read against the opposite ground and
apply only inside @media print.

subject: Isolate failures per surface, and make a task sheet printable
body:
A single root error boundary means one broken surface blanks the whole page and
takes the navigation with it. The station, the foundry and the run page now
catch their own, keep the operator where they are, name what failed, and offer
retry or leave. Each logs to the console rather than being swallowed by the
boundary that rendered it.

The task page is a work order — an instruction, a rate, a tolerance, a par time
— and now prints as one: ink back on white, screen-only chrome dropped, and
explorer links printing their destination, because a printed hash with nowhere
to go is not verifiable by anyone.

Idempotency on submit was already covered twice and is left alone: the row's
primary key is the trajectory hash, and the contract reverts AlreadySubmitted on
a hash it has seen. Verified on chain — trajectoryUsed returns true for a
recorded run, so a double-click cannot double-pay.

subject: Show placement while there is still time to act on it
body:
Two moments in a run had no feedback at all.

The placement term is 55% of the score and the operator learned it only after
letting go. A second ring now reads the payload's live distance from the datum:
inside the 25 mm band it closes on the payload and turns green, outside it sits
on the tolerance in red. Not decoration — it is the largest term in the score,
drawn while it can still be changed.

The moment of capture was the other: the payload simply started moving with the
tool and nothing said why. The jaws now take the signal colour while they are
actually holding something, driven by the same held flag the scorer uses.

subject: Restore fmtMon on the leaderboard
body:
Dropping an unused import from the new operator page, I stripped the same name
from the leaderboard, where it is used twice. next build reports 'Compiled
successfully' and then 'Failed to type check' as separate lines, and I read the
first and deployed on it.

subject: Give every contributor a page
body:
The leaderboard says who is ahead; the portfolio needs the operator's own wallet
connected. Neither lets you look a contributor up — which is what a buyer does
when deciding whether a corpus is worth paying for, and what a contributor does
when they want a link to their own work.

Both halves are public and neither is ours to assert: the accepted runs from the
ledger, and every call the address has made from Avalanche's own index,
including the reverted ones a ledger of accepted runs cannot show. Leaderboard
rows now point at it.

subject: Let one run be downloaded as one episode
body:
The corpus export takes a whole task. A page that shows a single run should be
able to hand you that run as data — the same samples the hash is derived from,
in the shape a loader expects, so the file can be checked against the chain
without downloading everything else recorded against the task.

subject: Remove the opengraph image: it 404s in production
body:
The route built locally, appeared in the routes manifest and produced output in
.next/server/app, and returned 404 on the deployed host — with and without a
pinned runtime. metadataBase, which the tag genuinely does require, is kept
because it is correct regardless.

Reverted rather than left in place: a share card that 404s is worse than none,
and reporting it as built would be false. Worth another attempt with a static
image or a different generation path, not with more guesses at the convention.

subject: Drop the runtime pin on the opengraph route
Set metadataBase, without which no og:image is emitted at all
body:
The opengraph route built and served, and the page carried no og:image tag:
Next cannot resolve a file-convention image to an absolute URL without
metadataBase, and drops the tag rather than failing. The card looked configured
and unfurled to nothing.

Caught by fetching the tag rather than trusting that the route existed.

subject: Give the share card the live numbers
body:
A link to this project unfurled into nothing. It now carries the task, run and
policy counts read from the contract at render time — because the whole claim is
that the figures are real and checkable, and a share card quoting numbers nobody
could verify would be the one place the product lied. If the chain cannot be
reached it renders without them rather than with invented ones.

subject: Rate-limit uploads by wallet, not by caller IP
body:
The first attempt keyed on x-forwarded-for and limited nothing: requests reach
this service through a proxy whose egress address changes per request, so every
upload landed in a fresh bucket. Seven in a row all went through, which is how
it was caught — by firing seven, not by reading the code.

The uploading wallet is the actor that actually claims the upload and it is
stable, so the bucket is keyed on that. The check sits after the address is
parsed and before anything is validated or written, which is where the real
cost is.

subject: Make the health checks readable by a person
body:
/api/health already checked the seven things that have to be true for a run to
be recorded and paid, and returned JSON to whoever thought to curl it. The same
checks now have a page, refreshed every fifteen seconds, with what each one
means when it fails — an unsigned score the contract will not pay, an EIP-712
domain mismatch that reverts every submission, a stored ledger that has drifted
from the contract's own count.

If the endpoint itself does not answer, the page says so rather than showing
nothing, because that is its own answer.

subject: Name the three ways this app can be unusable
body:
A degraded RPC looked like an empty protocol, an offline tab looked like a
broken page, and a wallet on the wrong chain looked like a wallet that would not
connect. Each now says which it is and offers the one action that fixes it — a
network switch, the faucet — instead of leaving the operator to guess.

The chain check asks the RPC directly rather than inferring from a page that
happens to be empty, and waits for two consecutive failures, because one dropped
request on a public endpoint is normal.

Also adds security headers with a CSP that names the only two origins this app
talks to besides itself, and a rate limit on the props upload — storing
multi-megabyte binaries on the same volume as the trajectory ledger is the most
expensive thing an anonymous caller can ask for.

subject: Show a buyer the corpus before they pay for it
body:
A licence buys a set of trajectories and the page asked for the money without
showing them. The export is thousands of frames, too much to fetch just to
decide, so this summarises the same rows the export ships — settled runs on the
active chain, so the summary describes the file that would actually arrive and
not a larger set.

Episodes, frames, distinct contributors, the score distribution across the
payable range, mean deviation and total recorded time, all from the rows
themselves.

subject: Let a task's own runs describe it
body:
The funder sets difficulty when they post, which is a guess. The runs are
evidence: the mean score operators actually achieve, mapped onto the same 1-5
scale, shown beside what the funder said.

Deliberately not a pass rate. A run that misses the datum is never written to
the chain, so failures leave no record and the denominator is not knowable —
publishing one would mean inventing it. The page says so where the number sits.

Fill pace comes from the run timestamps, and is withheld below three runs or a
five-minute span, because a burst inside a minute says nothing about how long
the rest will take.

subject: Show an operator what a run costs them
body:
Nobody shows the operator their margin. Fuji settles at 160 wei a gas unit —
confirmed against a receipt's effectiveGasPrice rather than assumed, because
reading Glacier's gasPrice as gwei overstates the fee by a factor of a billion —
so recording a run costs about 0.000000065 AVAX against the 0.005 it pays.

That is the concrete answer to the constraint PRODUCT.md names: first-run cost
has to be near zero, and it is. The portfolio now totals gas paid across every
call from the indexer's own figures, beside what those calls earned.

subject: Let the browser check the hash itself
body:
The run page already said whether the stored samples re-hash to the value on
chain — computed on our server, which is the thing being checked marking its own
homework. The canonical form moved out of lib/server so the browser can run the
same keccak over the samples it was handed and say so independently.

Verified outside the app entirely: a standalone script against the public API
reproduces 0x05e918d5... exactly.

subject: Say where a run's points went, and what they cost
body:
A score is one number and an operator cannot act on it. Every term is already
computed with the weight it carries, so the loss attributes exactly: the points
each part gave up, what those points were worth in AVAX at this task's rate, the
measurement behind it, and the one thing that would change it. A rejected run
also says how far short of the 40.00 pay threshold it fell.

Nothing is estimated — it is the arithmetic the contract was asked to pay
against, read backwards.

subject: Play the run back, in the room it was recorded in
body:
The ledger could tell you a run scored 0.83 and paid 0.004 AVAX. It could not
show you the run — the page had a two-dimensional trace of where the payload
went and nothing else.

Every sample already carried the six joint angles and the jaw opening, so the
arm can be posed straight from the recording rather than re-simulated. What the
scrubber drives is the trajectory the contract paid for, using the same samples
the hash is derived from: what is on screen is what would re-hash. Verified
against a real run — 181 samples, all six joints present in every one, and the
pose genuinely travels across the recording.

The scene comes from the same catalogue every other surface reads, so a replay
cannot show a different object from the station that recorded it.

Also adds IDEAS.md: 100 ranked ideas scored impact x feasibility x fit,
including the ones deliberately rejected and why — a token system and a trained
policy demo both contradict the pitch rather than extend it.

subject: Draw the props and the room at the size they are
body:
The station showed the arm and nothing else. Not a loading failure and not a
missing model — every prop was being rendered at 0.1 x 0.1 pixels and the room
at 1 x 1.

cad/kernel.py applies MM = 0.001 once at export, so every GLB in this project is
already in metres: a 42 mm dice is 0.042 units across. Prop scaled by
targetM / widthMm and Room by 0.001, both treating the files as millimetre-unit
and shrinking them a thousandfold. The arm was the only model nothing rescaled,
which is why it was the only thing on screen.

Every test this project has passed still passed while that was true — the assets
returned 200, the console was silent, the scene graph was right. So this adds
scripts/projected-size.mjs, which projects each model's real vertex bounds
through the station's own camera and reports the pixel footprint. It needs no
browser, which is the whole point: the frame loop stops in a background tab, so
nothing that depends on rendering could ever have caught this. It reports
0.1 x 0.1 px before and 54 x 58 px after.

The preview tiles are drawn per tile again. The single shared drei View renderer
was meant to keep 43 tiles inside the browser's WebGL context budget, and it
drew nothing at all — the inventory came back blank. A canvas per tile, mounted
only while the tile is within 300 px of the viewport, bounds the live contexts
to what is on screen instead of to the size of the library.

START also sat at 88% of the arm's maximum reach, where the elbow is nearly
straight and the tool swings a long way for a small pointer movement, with a
0.46 m haul to the goal. Both ends now sit in the middle of the envelope, 0.33 m
apart, inside the camera frame.

subject: Record test plan v2 results: 34 pass, 0 fail, 4 untestable
Make the station's controls reachable without a keyboard
body:
The controls overlay opened only on "?" — and the sidebar's "? All controls" was
a key hint, not a control. On the one page most likely to be driven by a mouse
or a trackpad, the list of what the keys do was itself behind a key. It is now a
button, and the shortcut still works.

The overlay is a modal and now says so: role="dialog", aria-modal, and a label.

Drops the "the same, on the arrows" row, which became redundant once the reach
and swing rows started naming the arrows themselves.

subject: Keep the landing page to one h1
body:
The hero is four sheets and each carried an h1, so the document had four
top-level headings. Three are inert and aria-hidden, so only one was ever
exposed to assistive technology — but the document outline is read by more than
a screen reader, and "one h1" is not a rule that bends because the extras are
hidden.

The sheet that is showing is the page's heading; the others are demoted to h2
while they wait. Under reduced motion, where all four are stacked and visible at
once, the first is the heading and the rest follow it.

Also adds TESTPLAN-V2.md — the surface the first plan did not reach: interaction,
the network tab per item, responsive, accessibility, mid-flow interruption,
empty states, and whether one task renders the same on every surface that draws it.

subject: Record the test-plan results: 59 pass, 0 fail, 1 untestable
Stop the station waiting for a task that will never arrive
body:
/station/9999 sat on "Reading task #9999 from the chain…" indefinitely. The
catalogue had already answered — eight tasks, none of them 9999 — so nothing was
still being read, and the page said otherwise for as long as you left it open.
The task page distinguishes loading from not-found; the station only ever
checked whether it had a task yet.

It now waits only while the catalogue is genuinely in flight, and otherwise says
the id is not in the registry, through the Missing component that was already
there for the other two cases.

subject: Send the trajectory's chain, which the run page already expected
body:
/run/[hash] types chainId, links the transaction with txUrlOn(chainId) and
renders a "settled on" note when the row belongs to a previous deployment — but
the API never sent the field. An archived Monad run therefore fell back to the
current chain and rendered a Snowtrace link for a transaction Fuji has never
heard of: the same defect the feed had, one page over, on the page whose whole
job is letting someone check a payout.

The edit that was meant to add this reported success earlier and did not apply.
Caught by testing the endpoint rather than re-reading the diff.

Also adds TESTPLAN.md — every page, route, on-chain call, integration and edge
case, each with what correct means as a specific result.

subject: Record the completion audit: 41/47 to 46/47
Close the honesty and vocabulary gaps the product's own spec names
body:
PRODUCT.md is a set of claims, and four of them were not true.

The arm was described as 7-DoF; it has six revolute axes, which is what the
dataset export, the spec sheet and the name THENAR-6 all say. The prop library
was described as sixteen; it is thirty-four, plus seven rooms. The keyboard
mapping listed keys the station does not bind. All three now say what the code
does.

The skill vocabulary — pick, place, stack, rotate, transfer, arrange, insert,
separate, reach — is named in PRODUCT.md as something that must survive into the
interface, and it was absent entirely. It is now derived from the instruction
the contract stores, the same way the payload, the landmark and the room are, so
it stays recoverable from chain state instead of living in a side table. Specific
cues beat the generic verb: almost every instruction begins "put", so matching on
position alone made every task a `place` and the vocabulary carried nothing.
Verified across the eight real on-chain instructions plus three others — eight of
the nine skills resolve, correctly.

The hub said nothing about who funded its tasks. All eight came from the address
that deployed the protocol, and the product's own rule is that anything shown
before real traffic exists is labelled rather than left to look like demand. The
hub now counts that from chain data and says so, and a task page says it on the
task.

The non-capabilities were named only in PRODUCT.md, never in the interface —
Principle 5 says the opposite. The spec sheet now carries them.

PasskeyRegistry was listed under "confirmed and shipping" while appearing nowhere
in the app outside the ABI. There is now a flow: generate a non-extractable
P-256 key in the browser, bind its public coordinates to an address in one
transaction, and prove a fresh signature against it through the precompile — a
read, so it costs nothing. Verified against the deployed registry: a real
WebCrypto signature returns true, a tampered r returns false.

subject: Record the scene pass in DESIGN.md and PLAN.md
Preload the room, or it never loads at all
body:
The room resolved correctly and reached the viewport — the scene just never
asked for it. Everything inside the Canvas renders on an animation frame, so in
any tab the browser has deprioritised the arm, the payload and the room are all
still unrendered; the only reason the payload and landmark appeared at all is
that they are preloaded outside the Canvas. The room was left off that list, so
it was the one asset whose fetch depended on a frame that may never come.

Verified per task, and each station now pulls exactly its own four assets:
task 4 "rotate the dice" (play) loads dice, crate and play.glb; task 0
"toothpaste into the drawer" (bathroom) loads toothpaste, drawer and
bathroom.glb. The room comes from the scenario the contract stores, so it is
derivable from chain state alone.

subject: Fix the hero taking the landing page down, and stop it depending on frames
body:
Deriving the scroll-linked opacity stops arithmetically put the first sheet's
arrival at a negative offset. The Web Animations API rejects that outright
rather than clamping, so motion threw on mount and the whole landing page fell
through to its error boundary — shipped, and caught in the browser rather than
by the build, which compiled it happily.

The sheet index now comes from the scroll event itself instead of a
scroll-linked motion value, which is both what "pagination" actually means and
what survives a browser that has stopped handing out animation frames. The
throttle went the same way: requestAnimationFrame around the handler
reintroduced exactly the dependency being removed, so geometry is cached on
resize and the scroll path reads nothing but scrollY.

Inactive sheets are now inert as well as transparent. They share one grid cell
with the visible one, so their links stayed clickable and stayed in the tab
order underneath the sheet actually on screen.

Verified in the browser at five scroll positions: the rail tick and the visible
sheet agree every time, and exactly three of the four are inert throughout.

subject: Give every task a room, and draw the library through one renderer
body:
The scenario has been a uint8 on the contract since the first deployment and it
changed a word in the sidebar and nothing else — a workshop task and a kitchen
task were recorded against the same bare grey table. There are now seven rooms,
one per scenario, generated from named dimensions by the same kernel that makes
the arm. Choosing a room when posting a task is choosing that index, so the room
is recoverable from chain state alone and no off-chain table can disagree with
what the station later draws.

The prop library goes from 16 to 34: twelve more payloads and six more
landmarks, so an instruction can name something other than the same ten
objects. All 42 models validate as glTF 2.0, and the eleven instructions in the
catalogue still resolve to the right pair.

Previews used to be one <Canvas> each, which is one WebGL context each. The
inventory shows the whole library and the post form shows everything you can
choose between: 43 contexts on a page, against a browser limit nearer 16. Past
that line the browser drops the oldest context and tiles go black in creation
order. They now draw through a single shared renderer — 43 tiles, one context,
measured in the browser. Its container needs pointer-events set inline, because
react-three-fiber writes its own and a full-viewport layer that takes clicks
would make every tile beneath it unclickable.

Tasks are resolved once, in a provider, rather than separately by the hub, the
floor, the task page and the station — which could each have drawn the same task
differently. Nothing is stored: the scene stays a pure function of chain state.

The hero is now a scroll-driven sequence. The instrument stays put and the scale
moves past it, which is the relationship a dial indicator has with the part it
reads. It is a real scroll rather than a hijacked one — four viewports and a
sticky frame — so the scrollbar tells the truth, find-in-page works, and reduced
motion gets the same words as an ordinary stacked page.

Also fixes a lie the type system was covering: `claimed` in the prop resolver
was declared number[] while holding [start, end] spans, with two `any` casts
hiding it.

subject: PLAN.md: record what was actually executed, and what was not
Break out the snapshot's row counts so 61 is never read as the feed's 12
Take the corpus somewhere the volume is not
body:
The trajectories are the only thing here that cannot be rebuilt. The chain
holds every hash, score and payment, but the samples that earned them exist in
one SQLite file on one Railway volume — so the moment that volume goes, every
payout on the site stops being auditable and the dataset the whole project is
about is gone.

Nightly now, into object storage in another region, on its own schedule after
the reconciler. The copy is made with VACUUM INTO rather than by reading the
file: under WAL the file on disk is not a consistent database on its own, and a
backup that restores to a corrupt page is worse than no backup because it is
believed. Each snapshot reports its own sha256 and the row counts it captured,
so a restore can be checked against what was meant to be in it.

SigV4 is signed by hand. The AWS SDK is several megabytes to issue one PUT.

subject: Put other operators in the room
body:
A station has always been one person alone with a scene. This makes each open
task a room: your tool position goes up six times a second and everyone else's
comes back in the same round trip, so you can see where the other hands are and
whether they are carrying anything while you drive your own run.

Presence is deliberately memory-only and deliberately not authoritative.
Nothing here is scored, paid or written to a chain — the trajectory is still
recorded locally and verified by signature, so a run measures identically with
the room empty and no operator can affect another's measurement by lying to
this. Losing it on a restart costs nothing.

Watching needs no wallet, which makes spectating the same code path as
operating with nothing to report yet. The floor at /space lists the rooms
busiest first, and keeps listing a room that has people in it even when the
task is full — hiding those meant the floor could say two operators were here
and show nowhere they were.

Ghosts render as an open marker with a dropped line to the table rather than a
second arm; six full manipulators is unreadable. Scene coordinates are
(x, z, -y) from the robot frame, the same mapping the payload uses. Rig is
given every prop except presence so the scene does not reconcile at 6 Hz.

Verified: two operators see each other with correct carry state and position, a
spectator with no wallet sees both, explicit leave is immediate, a silent
operator is pruned after four seconds, and four malformed poses are each
rejected with their own error.

subject: Close two more paths that ignored which chain a run settled on
body:
The feed, the standings and the task pages were scoped in the previous commit,
but two surfaces build their own queries and were missed.

The dataset export was the worse of the two: it selected every row for a task
regardless of chain or settlement, so a buyer downloading a corpus would get
episodes whose transaction field points at a chain the protocol no longer
writes to, mixed in with ones that verify. A corpus you cannot audit is the
one thing this project cannot ship.

The run page linked every transaction to the current chain's explorer, so an
archived run rendered a Snowtrace URL for a Monad transaction. It now links the
chain the row records and says plainly which deployment paid it.

Also puts the reconciler on a schedule. Nothing was calling it, so a row could
sit unverified indefinitely and the ledger could drift without anyone noticing
until it reached the feed. Vercel's scheduler only issues GET, hence the second
handler; every write it makes is a fact a chain returned, so an unsolicited
call can only re-confirm the truth.

subject: Read settlement history from Avalanche's own index
body:
Everything the portfolio showed arrived through this deployment: our RPC calls,
our database's transaction hashes. A page that says "verify this payout"
depended on a server we happen to be running, and on a ledger that by
construction only holds runs the contract accepted.

Glacier is Avalanche's indexer. Given an address it returns that address's
transactions against the protocol directly, so the history survives our
infrastructure disappearing, and it includes the calls that reverted. Selectors
are resolved through the ABI rather than a hand-written table — 22 settlements
for the deployer decode as 11 submitTrajectory, 8 createTask, 2 mintPolicy (one
reverted, shown as reverted) and the contract deployment itself.

The free tier needs no key, so there is no new credential.

Also stops the station claiming a run has not begun while the button beside it
reads END RUN: the live-placement panel now follows the run's own phase rather
than waiting on a frame that a throttled tab never delivers.

subject: Scope every stored run to the chain it settled on
body:
The feed reported 25 runs while the contract reported 12. The other 13 were
recorded under the previous deployment on Monad and came across with the
database, and they were rendered beside current runs with "verify" links to
Snowtrace — where those transactions do not exist. The oldest of them,
0x0777ad35, resolves on Monad at block 55922119 and nowhere on Fuji.

Rows now carry the chain they settled on. It is left NULL rather than
defaulted to the current chain, because guessing is what put unverifiable
transactions on the feed in the first place; /api/reconcile establishes it by
offering each hash to every chain this deployment has used and recording the
one that returns a receipt. The feed, the standings and the task pages read
only the active chain, and /api/health now fails outright when the stored
count and the contract's own trajectoryCount disagree.

The Monad runs are kept, not deleted — they happened and their operators were
really paid — and shown at /archive against the explorer that can verify them.

Also fixes two GSAP selectors that matched nothing: the hero paragraph never
carried data-anim="hero-copy", and DimRule only emitted data-anim="rule" from
its noted branch, so every plain rule on the landing page was invisible to the
timeline that claims to draw it. Eight console warnings on every load.

subject: Drop the header's backdrop blur, and name the right chain in DESIGN.md
body:
Scanning computed styles on the live pages rather than the source turned up
one thing the source scan could not: a backdrop-blur on the sticky header.
DESIGN.md's binding anti-references ban backdrop blur outright, and the bar
was already 95% opaque, so a 2px blur behind it bought nothing visible while
being the exact pattern the system forbids. The header is solid now.

DESIGN.md's own description still said 'get paid on Monad', and the signal
token was documented as carrying MON figures. Both say Avalanche.

subject: Put the prop tiles back on the documented type ramp
body:
The detector caught four literal font sizes in the two components added
today — 9px, 10px and 11px, none of them steps in DESIGN.md. The rest of the
codebase was clean, so this was my drift, not the system's.

They are on the label step now. That made the captions too wide for the tile
counts I had chosen, which is a layout problem rather than a type one: the
picker drops from eight columns to six and the strip from six to a stacked
name-over-role, so a 12px caption has room at every breakpoint instead of
shrinking type until it fits.

subject: Preload a task's props instead of waiting for the first frame
body:
The arm is preloaded at module scope; the payload and the landmark were not,
so they were only fetched once the canvas rendered. On a station opened in a
tab that is not compositing they were never fetched at all, and even in a
normal tab the scene popped in a beat after the arm.

subject: Show that the section nav scrolls on a narrow screen
body:
The scrollbar is hidden by design, which left Leaderboard and Foundry sitting
past the fold on a phone with nothing indicating they existed. They were always
reachable — the nav is overflow-x auto and scrolling reveals them — but a cue
you cannot see is not a cue. A mask fades the last 28px below the md
breakpoint, and does nothing above it.

subject: Let a task be posted against an uploaded model
body:
The upload endpoint stored models nothing could ever select: /post read only
the sixteen built-in props, so a funder's own GLB went into the volume and

subject: Refresh the Avalanche audit against a deployment that now settles
body:
The first version was written the day the app moved chains and said Avalanche
was 'not used'. That was too blunt. Six contracts are now Sourcify-verified on
Fuji, a trajectory settles and pays in one transaction, and a licence fans out
to its cap table — the chain is used properly.

What has not changed is the finding a judge on this track cares about: every
call goes over generic C-Chain JSON-RPC. Glacier, Teleporter, Warp, subnets,
eERC and ICTT are all untouched. The question is not whether the app works on
Avalanche, it is whether it needed to be.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: A sponsor audit you can run against any name
body:
Five audits in docs/ answer 'is X used here' for the technologies this project
actually contains. This is the instrument that produced them, so the sixth
answer costs one command instead of an afternoon.

The naive version — grep for the sponsor's name — reports every deeply used
library as absent, because nothing that uses viem writes 'viem' on the call
line. It now reads the symbols imported from a matching package and looks for
calls to those, which is what usage actually looks like. Config files are
scanned too: leaving them out made a service the entire API proxies to look
like it was never mentioned.

Validated against seven answers established by hand: viem, three and rainbowkit
come back GENUINELY USED; walletconnect, Avalanche and railway come back PROSE
ONLY; glacier, never integrated, comes back ABSENT. Every one matches.

It stops short of the part that needs a person, and says so: a call site is not
proof the flow reaches it, so the browser check is still on you.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Audit Railway and Vercel — the two that are actually used
body:
Every other sponsor audit in this folder found imported, absent or generic.
These two are different. Railway is load-bearing: AXON_DB_PATH points at a
volume holding every trajectory, every signature and every uploaded model, and
20 trajectories plus 1 prop survived today's 09:09 redeploy. next.config.ts
names the reason a serverless host cannot do this job.

Vercel is genuinely used and genuinely replaceable, and it gets no fifty-item
list. Nothing it offers beyond what is already in use would strengthen this
product, and inventing fifty ways to use it would be the checkbox integration
these audits exist to call out.

The honest finding is durability: SQLite on a single volume currently holds the
only copy of the asset this project sells.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Audit WalletConnect/Reown: imported, disabled, and mobile cannot connect
body:
RainbowKit is a dependency and lib/wagmi.ts imports walletConnectWallet,
metaMaskWallet and rainbowWallet — none are offered. The projectId the group
is gated on is set nowhere: not in vercel.json, not on the Railway service,
not in any .env. Verified live on thenar.io/hub, the connect modal offers
Browser Wallet and Coinbase only, with zero requests to any relay host.

The code is honest about it rather than faking it, which is the right call for
a missing credential. But the cost has not been accounted for: injectedWallet
needs an extension and mobile browsers do not have one, so an operator on a
phone cannot connect at all — on a product whose audience is 'anyone with a
browser and no robotics hardware'.

The strongest organic fit is not the modal, it is smart sessions. The contract
caps an operator at five runs and PRODUCT.md says the work should feel closer
to a rhythm game than data entry; five wallet signatures per sitting is the
friction everyone accepts and nobody fixes.

Everything here needs a free projectId from cloud.reown.com, which I cannot
create. Reported rather than worked around.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Audit Monad against what the app runs today, and rank 50 uses
body:
MONAD.md and MONAD-2.md audited the Monad deployment and are accurate about
it. This audits thenar.io as it runs now, on Avalanche, and asks what going
back would buy — measured over 20 blocks on each chain rather than asserted.

Monad is 0.30s per block against Fuji's 4.95s, and carries a 150M block gas
limit against 32M. That matters here for one specific reason: PRODUCT.md
defines success as an operator seeing payment arrive before they let go of the
mouse, and a 4.95s mean block time makes that unreachable. The strongest
argument for Monad in this project is arithmetic, not preference.

It also corrects MONAD.md on its own headline: the P-256 precompile is not a
Monad differentiator. Fuji answers the identical call identically — verified
by signing with WebCrypto on both chains. eth_getCode cannot test a precompile,
which is how I got this wrong in the first place.

Monad usage in the running app is zero. The sharded slot counters in
AxonProtocol are the one Monad-shaped decision that survives, and on a chain
that executes serially they buy nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: The passkey path works on Avalanche — I tested it wrong
body:
I reported PasskeyRegistry as inert on Fuji and wrote that into PRODUCT.md as
a non-capability and into the Avalanche audit as a missing precompile. Both
were wrong, and the method was the problem: eth_getCode is meaningless for a
precompile, which has no bytecode and always answers empty.

Called properly — a real WebCrypto secp256r1 signature against the deployed
registry at 0x82aE3011…6BCE9F — Fuji returns 1 for a valid signature and 0
when one byte of r is changed. Same on Monad. The capability is real on both.

Separately, the app was still sending operators to faucet.monad.xyz from three
places while settling in AVAX. The faucet is now FAUCET_URL in lib/chain.ts,
beside the explorer, for the same reason the ticker moved there.

And the README still advertised the Monad contracts as the live deployment. It
now names the Fuji addresses and their Sourcify status, keeps the Blitz result
because it happened, and marks MONAD.md and MONAD-2.md as historical rather
than deleting a record of real work.
